title: Beyond “From” and “Received”: Exploring the Dynamics of Email Triage
research_question: How do information workers actually triage accumulated email, what determines which messages they handle first, and what additional information could email interfaces expose to support that process?
methodology: The authors conduct contextual interviews with ten information workers and then survey 2,000 randomly selected employees within the same company, obtaining 233 responses. All participants use Microsoft Outlook, and survey respondents are grouped into low-, medium-, and high-volume triagers according to daily email volume. The study measures preprocessing practices, conversation grouping, sequential versus priority processing, single- versus multi-pass strategies, which emails are handled first, and when triage occurs during the day.

key_findings.finding: Unread inbox messages and messages received today were rated the most important categories to include during triage, both averaging 4.4 on the study's five-point scale.
Users did not share a single priority policy: 19 percent reported priority-only triage, 30 percent sequential-only triage, and 15 percent reported using both approaches.
Multi-pass triage was more common than single-pass triage, with 47 percent reporting multi-pass only versus 17 percent single-pass only under the authors' combined-question criterion.
Many multi-pass users first removed low-importance or junk messages because they were quick to process and because clearing them made important messages easier to find.
Message importance depended substantially on the user's current social and work context, including schedule, close collaborators, active projects, and project role.
High-volume users triaged email more frequently throughout the day than low-volume users and were more likely to perform triage outside core work periods.

The authors recommend exposing socially salient sender, receiver, recency, and contextual metadata to help users foreground important mail or clear unimportant mail, but the study does not experimentally validate such an interface.

limitations: All interview and survey participants are employees of one company and all use Microsoft Outlook.
The observational sample includes only ten contextual-interview participants, while most other evidence is self-reported survey behavior.
The study was conducted in 2005, before many current email, chat, mobile-notification, and machine-learning interface conventions.
The work studies triage behavior rather than implementing or evaluating a prioritization or briefing algorithm.
The proposed socially salient interface features are design implications rather than experimentally tested interventions.
The study does not determine how message importance changes after a fact is resolved or superseded.
It does not study incremental summarization, information deduplication, or explicit maintenance of still-open state across successive briefings.
raw_claims: The study defines email triage as reviewing unhandled email and deciding what to do with it.
Ten information workers participated in contextual interviews.
A survey was sent to 2,000 randomly selected employees and received 233 responses.
Higher-volume email users used preprocessing rules more heavily.
Conversation grouping was not commonly used by the studied users.
Unread inbox mail and mail received today received the highest importance ratings for triage inclusion.
Some users processed messages sequentially while others used explicit priority-based passes.
Multi-pass triage was more common than single-pass triage among survey respondents under the authors' classification.
Users sometimes handled low-importance mail before high-importance mail because it was fast to delete or file.
The importance of a message varied with current projects, relationships, role, schedule, and recency.
High-volume users performed triage at more times during the day.
Participants asked for ways to keep important items visible and for better task-management support.
The authors argue that email interfaces should expose more socially salient information for sorting and searching.
